actions.justification: Mandatory first step: patient presents with tachycardia (HR 105), hypotension (BP 98/60), and melena — immediate vital signs assessment required per ACG GI bleeding guideline.
Mandatory: patient shows signs of hemodynamic instability (MAP 73, HR 105, BP 98/60). Hemodynamic assessment must be performed immediately to guide resuscitation per ACG guideline.
Mandatory: large-bore IV access is essential for fluid resuscitation and medication administration in this hemodynamically unstable GI bleeding patient.
Mandatory: Assess hemoglobin/hematocrit and platelet count to guide transfusion decisions in active GI bleeding.
Mandatory: Patient is on warfarin - INR/PT critical to assess anticoagulation status and guide reversal strategy, especially with mechanical mitral valve complicating reversal decisions.
Mandatory: Patient is hemodynamically unstable with melena - type and crossmatch required for potential packed RBC transfusion.

Patient is hemodynamically unstable (BP 98/60, HR 105, MAP 73). ACG guidelines mandate hemodynamic resuscitation before endoscopy. IV crystalloid bolus is the immediate intervention to stabilize perfusion.
IV PPI is standard of care for upper GI bleeding (melena presentation) to reduce acid and promote clot stability at the bleeding site.

Early GI consultation is essential for endoscopy planning. This patient will require urgent endoscopy once hemodynamically stabilized. Also, the patient's mechanical mitral valve makes anticoagulation reversal decisions complex — GI input is critical.
BMP assesses renal function, electrolytes, and BUN/creatinine ratio (elevated BUN suggests upper GI bleeding source). Critical given hemodynamic instability (BP 98/60, HR 105).
Lactate quantifies degree of tissue hypoperfusion/shock in this hemodynamically unstable patient (MAP 73, HR 105, BP 98/60). Guides resuscitation adequacy.

Patient is hemodynamically unstable with likely significant blood loss and on warfarin with mechanical mitral valve — crossmatch for packed RBCs and FFP (to reverse warfarin) is urgent. Note: type and crossmatch was done but order_type_and_crossmatch is listed as available and distinct from order_lab_type_and_crossmatch already completed — selecting to ensure crossmatch (not just type and screen) is confirmed for transfusion readiness.

Patient is hemodynamically unstable (HR 105, BP 98/60). Repeat CBC is needed to trend hemoglobin levels and guide transfusion decisions, especially since initial CBC is pending and clinical picture suggests significant blood loss.

Patient is hemodynamically unstable with tachycardia and hypotension consistent with significant hemorrhage. Transfusion with packed RBCs is indicated if Hgb <7 (or higher threshold given mechanical valve) to restore oxygen-carrying capacity and hemodynamic stability prior to endoscopy.

Pre-endoscopy prokinetic (e.g., erythromycin or metoclopramide) is indicated per ACG guidelines for upper GI bleeding to improve gastric visualization by clearing blood and clots from the stomach before urgent endoscopy.

Patient is hemodynamically unstable (HR 105, BP 98/60, MAP 73) with ongoing upper GI bleeding. Trending lactate will assess tissue perfusion and adequacy of resuscitation efforts, guiding further management.

Initial CBC is pending; repeating ensures timely hemoglobin result to guide transfusion decisions. Patient is on warfarin with a mechanical mitral valve — accurate hemoglobin and platelet counts are critical before any procedural intervention.

Patient has massive upper GI bleed on warfarin with hemodynamic instability and a mechanical mitral valve. Early surgical consultation is prudent in case endoscopic therapy fails or emergent intervention is needed.

Octreotide reduces splanchnic blood flow and decreases portal pressure, which can help control upper GI bleeding. This patient has hemodynamic instability (HR 105, BP 98/60) with active melena. Octreotide is indicated as adjunctive therapy in upper GI bleeding while awaiting endoscopy, particularly if variceal source is possible.

CT abdomen can help localize the bleeding source and assess for complications (e.g., perforation, vascular abnormality) in this hemodynamically tenuous patient with upper GI bleeding on warfarin with a mechanical mitral valve, while endoscopy preparation is underway. This is an optional but clinically useful step to guide management.

If CT abdomen identifies active extravasation or if bleeding is refractory, angiography can serve both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes (embolization). Given ongoing hemodynamic instability (HR 105, BP 98/60) and the patient's anticoagulated state, having angiography queued is appropriate as a contingency for endoscopy failure or surgical risk mitigation.
Patient has hemodynamic instability (HR 105, BP 98/60) with dizziness - assess mental status/LOC as part of ongoing hemodynamic monitoring to detect deterioration requiring escalation of care.

Patient is on chronic warfarin with active upper GI bleeding. IV Vitamin K is indicated to reverse anticoagulation. Must be balanced against mechanical mitral valve thrombosis risk, but active hemorrhage takes priority; coagulation labs are pending to guide further reversal.

Patient is on warfarin with active upper GI hemorrhage and hemodynamic instability. Vitamin K IV has been given but onset is delayed (12-24h). FFP provides immediate factor replacement for urgent INR reversal. Mechanical mitral valve warrants caution but active life-threatening hemorrhage takes priority per ACG guidelines.
